issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: 'Comments on sexual violence' is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening accident in the absence of any sexual-trauma content elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals. This is not just unusual; it suggests a different trauma theme than the stated index event.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
issues.explanation: 'I dwell on how the event could have been prevented' can occur after accidents, but here the rest of the profile centers on sensory trauma cues and intrusive memory/avoidance rather than a coherent prevention-focused appraisal pattern. With Negative Appraisals absent and no threat/appraisal content linking to preventability, this strategy feels weakly grounded relative to the formulation and selected items.

vignette:
Rodrigo is a 62-year-old Colombian-American general surgeon, married for thirty-one years, who presented for his initial psychological evaluation approximately eight months after a serious motor vehicle accident that left him, in his own words, "changed in ways I cannot explain to my wife or to myself." He came to the intake appointment in pressed slacks and a collared shirt, composed in manner but visibly tense when the subject of the accident was raised, his hands settling into his lap with a deliberateness that suggested he had learned to manage what they might otherwise do.

The accident occurred on a Tuesday evening in late autumn when Rodrigo was driving home from the hospital after a twelve-hour shift. At an intersection he had crossed hundreds of times, a sedan ran a red light at speed and struck his vehicle on the driver's side. The impact was violent and immediate - the door caved inward, the airbag deployed, and Rodrigo found himself pinned briefly before he was able to push free. What he remembers most acutely from those minutes is the sensation of the deployed airbag fabric against his left hand and forearm - a dense, powdery roughness - and the sight of the other car crumpled against his, its hood accordioned, steam rising. A colleague from his hospital, a physician he recognised, happened to be among the first bystanders to reach him. Rodrigo recalls looking up and seeing that familiar face and feeling, inexplicably, a wave of shame rather than relief.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo returned to surgical practice as quickly as his attending physicians permitted, telling himself and his wife, Claudia, that work would restore his equilibrium. It did not. In the operating theatre, when a scrub technician passes him instruments, the texture of certain surgical drapes - a particular woven weave used in abdominal procedures - contacts his gloved hand and something in him lurches backward. The memory does not arrive as a recollection so much as an imposition: vivid, insistent, carrying a sensory weight that his memories of ordinary mornings or family dinners simply do not possess. He described it in session as feeling "more like the thing itself than a memory of the thing," and he has come to dread the unpredictability of its arrival. When it begins to surface he finds himself pressing it back before it can complete itself, turning his attention to the operative field with a ferocity that his residents have mistaken for intensity of focus.

Driving past damaged or wrecked vehicles - on the highway, in salvage yards visible from the road - stops him cold in a way he cannot fully account for. He has begun taking a longer route to the hospital that adds twenty minutes each way, and when Claudia asks why, he offers traffic as the reason. He has not told her the truth, and the distance this has introduced between them is something he notices but has not addressed. Claudia has remarked that he seems absent even when he is present, and she is not wrong.

Outside the hospital, Rodrigo has withdrawn from the things that once structured his leisure. He and Claudia used to hike on weekends; he has declined every invitation she has extended since the accident, citing fatigue. He resigned quietly from a recreational tennis league without explanation. When he considered the reason honestly in session, he acknowledged that the physical exertion - the elevated heart rate, the breathlessness, the bodily sensation of being pushed - felt intolerable to him now, though he struggled to articulate precisely why. He has also stopped attending the monthly dinners held by a group of physician friends, because one of those friends was the colleague who found him at the accident scene, and Rodrigo has not been able to look at that man without the intersection returning to him.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a moment in the operating room three weeks ago when, during a routine cholecystectomy, the memory arrived with such force that he paused mid-procedure for several seconds. A nurse asked if he was all right. He said yes. But he drove home that evening knowing that he could no longer manage this alone, and that the surgeon's reflex to push through had reached its limit. What he most fears is that something essential in him has been permanently altered. What he most hopes - though he said it quietly, as though he were not certain he deserved to hope it - is that he might find his way back.
